lead: A sensor notices a physical change; a transducer turns that change into an electrical signal an instrument or controller can read. The Hall effect does this with a magnetic field: a thin semiconductor carrying current produces a small transverse voltage when a magnet comes near. A proximity sensor does it without contact, switching its output when a metal, plastic or other target enters range. You meet both in a phone flip cover, a motor speed wheel, a card reader and a factory conveyor.
prereq: You need: magnetic flux density and the force on a moving charge from Unit 3, and the op-amp comparator from Unit 4; 6.1 reminds you how a deflection becomes a reading.

blocks.text: A sensor responds to a physical quantity such as temperature, light, pressure or magnetic field. A transducer converts one form of energy into another. An electrical transducer converts the physical quantity into a voltage, current or resistance change. Every sensor with an electrical output is a transducer. A loudspeaker is a transducer but not a sensor, because it converts electrical energy to sound, not the other way.
Transducers are grouped by how they get their output energy.

items: Active transducer: it generates its own voltage from the physical quantity. A thermocouple gives a small voltage from a temperature difference; a piezoelectric disc gives a voltage when pressed.
Passive transducer: it needs an external supply and changes its resistance, capacitance or voltage under that supply. A strain gauge, an RTD and a Hall element are passive.

blocks.text: The output may be analog (a continuous voltage, such as 0.04 V from a Hall element) or digital (a switch that is HIGH or LOW). A digital output is easier for a microcontroller to count, so many sensors include a comparator inside the package. The useful specifications are range (the physical span it can measure), sensitivity (output change per unit input), resolution (smallest detectable change), accuracy (closeness to the true value) and hysteresis (the difference between switch-on and switch-off points).

Take a thin rectangular slab of semiconductor. Pass a steady current I along its length. Apply a magnetic field B perpendicular to the face of the slab. The moving charge carriers feel a sideways force, so electrons pile up on one edge and leave positive charge on the other. This charge builds a transverse electric field until its force balances the magnetic force. The steady voltage across the width is the Hall voltage.

blocks.where: V<sub>H</sub> is the Hall voltage in volts (V); K<sub>H</sub> is the Hall sensitivity in V/(A·T); I is the current through the element in amperes (A); B is the magnetic flux density in tesla (T). For a slab of thickness t, carrier density n and carrier charge q, K<sub>H</sub> = 1/(n q t), so a thin, lightly doped semiconductor gives a larger voltage.

blocks.text: The sign of V<sub>H</sub> reverses when B reverses or when I reverses. That sign carries direction information: a north pole and a south pole give opposite readings. The voltage is small, often tens of millivolts, so the signal chain is: Hall element, amplifier, comparator. The amplifier raises the level and the comparator turns it into a clean HIGH or LOW at a chosen threshold. The figure shows this chain with the worked example's values.

Hall sensors measure magnetic field, and through it they measure speed, position and current. A toothed wheel or a ring of magnets on a motor shaft passes the sensor and produces one pulse per tooth or magnet. A phone flip cover uses a small magnet and a Hall switch to blank the screen. A clamp-type current sensor uses the field around a wire; no electrical connection to the wire is needed. Brushless DC motors use Hall sensors to know rotor position before switching the coils (see Unit 3, special machines).
A proximity sensor detects an object without touching it. The target comes within a rated distance, called the sensing range, and the output changes state. Three common types use different physics.

Inductive. A coil and oscillator create a high-frequency field at the face. A metal target nearby carries eddy currents, which load the oscillator and reduce its amplitude. A comparator detects the drop and switches the output. Inductive sensors detect metals only, with ranges of a few millimetres. They suit a steel can on a conveyor or a metal cam on a rotating shaft.

Capacitive. Two plates at the face form a capacitor with the air in front. Any material whose dielectric constant differs from air changes the capacitance when it enters the field. Capacitive sensors detect metal, plastic, glass, wood and even liquid level through a wall, with ranges up to about 25 mm.

Optical. An emitter sends light and a receiver looks for it. In through-beam types the target blocks the beam; in diffuse types the target reflects light back. Optical sensors see almost any object and reach much farther, but dust, rain or a transparent bottle can fool them.

The three-wire output is named after the transistor inside. An NPN output sinks current to 0 V when active, so the load connects between the output and the positive supply. A PNP output sources current from the positive supply when active, so the load connects between the output and 0 V. Reversing the expected type gives a load that never switches. Hysteresis makes the switch-on distance larger than the switch-off distance; without it, a target resting at the threshold would chatter. Signal conditioning is therefore an amplifier or oscillator, then a comparator with a small hysteresis band, as in Unit 4.

figure.caption: A steady current and a nearby magnet act on a thin semiconductor; the small Hall voltage is amplified and compared with a threshold to give a clean switch output. Notice that the magnetic field does the measuring, while the current only biases the element.

spec.title: Hall sensor signal chain
spec.aria: A constant current and a magnetic field act on a Hall element; its 40 mV Hall voltage is amplified by 100 and compared with a threshold to give a 4 V switch output.

examples.question: A Hall sensor has sensitivity K<sub>H</sub> = 20 V/(A·T). It carries a current I = 10 mA in a magnetic field B = 0.2 T. Find the Hall voltage in millivolts. The amplifier after it has a gain of 100; find the amplifier output.
steps: Write the given values with units: K<sub>H</sub> = 20 V/(A·T), I = 10 mA = 10 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A = 0.01 A, B = 0.2 T, gain A = 100.
Substitute: V<sub>H</sub> = 20 × 0.01 × 0.2. First 20 × 0.01 = 0.2 V/T; then 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04 V.
Amplifier output = gain × V<sub>H</sub> = 100 × 0.04 V = 4 V.
examples.answer: The Hall voltage is 0.04 V, that is 40 mV, and the amplifier output is 4 V.
examples.check:
K = 20
I_mA = 10
B = 0.2
gain = 100
VH_mV = K * I_mA * B
Vout = VH_mV * gain / 1000
print(VH_mV)
print(Vout)

traps: The Hall voltage reverses when either B or I reverses. A sign slip means the sensor reports the wrong pole or the wrong direction of rotation.
Inductive proximity sensors detect metals only; capacitive types detect non-metals too. An examiner often asks which one sees a plastic bottle.
Keep the units of K<sub>H</sub> as V/(A·T) and put I in amperes, not milliamperes. Substituting 10 instead of 0.01 gives an answer 1000 times too large.
Nominal sensing range is not the guaranteed operating point. Hysteresis and temperature drift mean you should work inside the range, not at its edge.
An NPN output sinks current and a PNP output sources current. Wiring the load to the wrong rail gives no switching and is a common lab mistake.

quiz.q: Define a sensor and a transducer. Give one example of each.
quiz.a: A sensor responds to a physical quantity, such as a thermistor responding to temperature. A transducer converts one form of energy into another, such as a loudspeaker converting electrical energy to sound.

quiz.q: Write the Hall voltage formula and state the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: V<sub>H</sub> = K<sub>H</sub> I B, where V<sub>H</sub> is in volts, K<sub>H</sub> in V/(A·T), I in amperes and B in tesla.

quiz.q: Why is a Hall voltage usually amplified before use?
quiz.a: The Hall voltage is only tens of millivolts because the charge separation is small. An amplifier raises it to a few volts so a comparator or microcontroller can read it without being troubled by noise and offset.

quiz.q: A Hall sensor has K<sub>H</sub> = 15 V/(A·T), carries I = 20 mA and sits in B = 0.1 T. Find V<sub>H</sub> in millivolts. With a gain of 50, find the output.
A motor shaft carries two magnets. A Hall sensor gives 60 pulses per second. Find the speed in rpm.
quiz.a: Two pulses per revolution. Revolutions per second = 60/2 = 30. Speed = 30 × 60 = 1800 rpm.

quiz.q: A plastic bottle and a steel can move on the same conveyor. Which proximity sensor detects both, and which detects only the can? Explain.
quiz.a: A capacitive sensor detects both, because plastic and steel both change the capacitance at its face. An inductive sensor detects only the steel can, because it needs eddy currents in a metal target.

quiz.q: Explain why a proximity switch uses hysteresis, and what would happen without it.
quiz.a: Hysteresis makes the switch-off distance smaller than the switch-on distance. Without it, a target resting near the threshold would make the output chatter between HIGH and LOW because of noise and small vibrations.

quiz.q: A PNP proximity sensor must drive a lamp. Explain how the lamp is connected and when it lights.
quiz.a: The lamp connects between the sensor output and 0 V. When a target is detected, the PNP transistor sources current from the positive supply through the output and the lamp, so the lamp lights.

beyond: Not for the exam. Inside real Hall switches, the element, amplifier, comparator and output transistor sit on one silicon chip, with chopping to cancel offset and temperature drift. Research moves toward magnetoresistive and giant magnetoresistive sensors, which give a larger change for the same field and are used in gear-tooth sensing and current measurement. Industrial proximity sensors increasingly carry IO-Link, a small serial link that reports distance and health besides the switch state. Capacitive sensing has moved into touch screens and water-level monitors. Useful searches: Hall effect sensor IC, GMR sensor, inductive proximity sensor eddy current, IO-Link sensor.
